parole.significato: A Japanese demon.
parole.testo: From Japanese 悪魔, from Middle Chinese 惡魔 (MC 'ak ma, literally “bad, evil + demon”).

parole.significato: Thrill-seeking; wild.
parole.testo: From Japanese 万歳(ばんざい) (banzai, “long live..., huzzah, hurrah”), from Middle Chinese 萬歲 (mjonᴴ sjwejᴴ), from Old Chinese 萬歲 (*mans s-qʷʰats, “10,000 years [of life]”, i.e. “immortality”), from 萬 /万 (wàn, “10,000”) 歲 /岁 (suì, “year (of age)”). Compare Mandarin 萬歲／万岁 (wànsùi).

parole.significato: An Asian aesthetic of young men whose beauty (and sex appeal) transcends the boundary of gender or sexual orientation,…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Japanese 美少年 (bishōnen びしょうねん), from Middle Chinese 美 (mij^X, “beautiful”) + 少年 (syewᴴ nen, “teenaged boy”) (compare Mandarin 少年 (shàonián)).

parole.significato: A quarterstaff, especially in an oriental context.
parole.testo: From Japanese 棒 (bō), from Middle Chinese 棒 (baewng^X, “staff, club”) (compare modern Chinese 棒 (bàng)).

parole.significato: A tree or plant that has been miniaturized by planting it in a small pot, restricting its roots, and by careful pruning.
parole.testo: From Japanese 盆栽 (bonsai), from Middle Chinese 盆 (MC bwon, “bowl”) + 栽 (MC tsoj|dzojH, “to plant”).

parole.significato: A member of a Japanese social minority group, descendants of feudal-era outcasts.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Japanese 部落民, from Middle Chinese 部落 (bu^X lak, “tribe”) + 民 (mjin, “people”).

parole.significato: An ethical code of the samurai that was prevalent in feudal Japan that advocated unquestioning loyalty to the master at…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Japanese 武(ぶ)士(し)道(どう) (bushidō), from Middle Chinese 武士 (mju^X dzri^X, “warrior”) + 道 (daw^X, “way”). Cognate with Mandarin 武士 (wǔshì) and Cantonese 武士 (mou⁵ si⁶).

parole.significato: A Buddhist shrine, comprising a wooden cabinet with doors that enclose and protect a religious icon.
parole.testo: From Japanese 仏壇 (ぶつだん butsudan), from Middle Chinese 佛 (bjot "Buddha") ＋ 壇 (dan "altar", "platform").

parole.significato: A lord during the Japanese feudal period.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Japanese 大(だい)名(みょう) (daimyō), from Middle Chinese 大名 (dajᴴ mjieng, “excellent one”), from 大 (“great”) + 名 (mjieng, “name”).

parole.significato: A diacritic (゛) used with Japanese kana to mark a consonant as voiced.
parole.testo: From Japanese 濁点(だくてん) (dakuten), from Middle Chinese 濁 (ɖæwk, “voiced, turbid”) + 點 (tém, “dot, mark”).

parole.significato: A thin mattress of tufted cotton or similar material, placed on a floor or on a raised, foldable frame as a bed.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Japanese 布団 (futon), in turn from Middle Chinese 蒲團 (MC bu dwan, “meditation cushion”) (compare Mandarin 蒲团 (pútuán)), from 蒲 (bu, “bulrush, cattail”) + 團 (dwan, “sphere, round object”) from the way the original cushion was round and made from woven bulrushes.

parole.significato: the ancient court ritual classical music of Japan, of Chinese origin
parole.testo: From Japanese 雅楽 (gagaku), from Middle Chinese 雅樂 (MC ngaeX ngaewk, “ancient ceremonial music”). Doublet of aak and yayue.

parole.significato: A non-Japanese person.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Japanese 外人 (gaijin, “foreigner”), from Middle Chinese 外人 (ngwajᴴ nyin). Compare Mandarin 外人 (wàirén), from Old Chinese 外人 (*ŋʷaːds njin, “foreigner, outsider” < “non-relative”), from 外 (wài, “outside, outer”) + 人 (rén, “person”).

parole.significato: A ritual gesture of Eastern origin, with hands pressed together in front of the chest. It can be used for prayer or as…
parole.testo: From Japanese 合掌 (gasshō), from Middle Chinese 合掌 (ɣop-tʃáng, “Buddhist-style pressed-palm gesture of piety”) (compare Mandarin 合掌 (hézhǎng), Cantonese 合掌 (hap⁶ jeung²)), from 合 (“unite”) and 掌 (zhǎng, “palm”).

parole.significato: A Japanese female entertainer skilled in various arts such as tea ceremony, dancing, singing and calligraphy.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Japanese 芸者(げいしゃ) (geisha, “artisan”), from Middle Chinese 藝 (MC ngjiejH, “art, craft”) + 者 (MC tsyaeX, “-er”).

parole.significato: The entryway to a Japanese house, where street shoes are removed and houseshoes put on before entering the house, and h…
parole.testo: From Japanese 玄関(げんかん) (genkan), from Middle Chinese 玄關 (MC hwen kwaen, literally “front door”).

parole.significato: Synonym of lilac daphne.
parole.testo: Maybe borrowed from Japanese 芫花 (genka), whose historical spelling is げんくわ (genkwa), ultimately comes from Middle Chinese 芫花 (MC ngjwon xwae, “lilac daphne”).

parole.significato: The taproot of young edible burdock plants (Arctium lappa), eaten as a root vegetable.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Japanese ごぼう, ゴボウ, 牛蒡 (gobō, “burdock (Arctium lappa); burdock root”), from Middle Chinese 牛蒡 (ŋɨu pɑŋ^X, “burdock”) (modern Mandarin 牛蒡 (niúbàng)), from 牛 (ŋɨu, “ox”) + 蒡 (pɑŋ^X, a word only appearing in the compound 牛蒡), possibly because oxen have been observed eating the leaves of t

parole.significato: Traditional Japanese fish printing.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Japanese 魚拓 (gyotaku, ぎょたく), from Middle Chinese 魚 (ngjo, “fish”) + 拓 (tʰak, “rubbing”).

parole.significato: A technique of using splashed ink in brushwork painting, especially for painting a landscape.
parole.testo: From Japanese 破墨 (haboku はぼく), from Middle Chinese 破 (pʰà "broken up") + 墨 (mok "ink") (compare Mandarin pòmò 破墨, Cantonese po³-mak⁶ 破墨).

parole.significato: A Japanese poem in three lines, the first and last consisting of five morae, and the second consisting of seven morae,…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Japanese 俳(はい)句(く) (haiku), from Middle Chinese 俳 (beaj, “paralleled [writing]”) + 句 (kɨoᴴ, “line”).

parole.significato: A breed of dog originating from Japan, resembling a spitz dog breed, although not officially ranked as a spitz dog bree…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Japanese 北(ほっ)海(かい)道(どう) (Hokkaidō, “North Sea Circuit”), from Middle Chinese 北海 (pək-hʌi˧˥, “Northern sea”) + 道 (dáu, “Circuit”, a province-like administrative unit from Tang dynasty China).

parole.significato: A Shinto place of worship.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Japanese 神社 (じんじゃ, jinja), from Middle Chinese 神社, from Old Chinese 神社 (“sacrificial altar, shrine”), from 神 (*hlin, “deity, divine”) + 社 (*ɦljaːʔ, “Earth deity [and altar]”). Cognate with Mandarin 神社 (shénshè, “shrine”).

parole.significato: A regional tour, undertaken between honbashos, during which the rikishi give exhibition matches.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Japanese 巡業 (じゅんぎょう, jungyō), from Middle Chinese 巡 (zwin, “to make rounds, tour”) + 業 (ngjæp, “work”).

parole.significato: The second highest division in sumo wrestling, below makuuchi and above makushita; rikishi at this point receive a sala…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Japanese 十両(じゅうりょう) (jūryō, “ten ryō”), from Middle Chinese 十 (dʒip, “ten”) + 兩 (ljáng, “tael”).

parole.significato: A fictional humanoid monster as a typical antagonist in tokusatsu media.
parole.testo: From Japanese 怪人 (かいじん, kaijin), from Middle Chinese 怪 (kweajᴴ, “strange, fantastic”) + 人 (nyin, “person”)

parole.significato: A fictional giant monster, particularly of the kind found in Japanese science fiction films and other media, like Godzi…
parole.testo: From Japanese 怪獣 (かいじゅう, kaijū), from Middle Chinese 怪 (kweajᴴ, “strange, fantastic”) + 獸 (syuwᴴ, “beast”) (compare Mandarin 怪獸 /怪兽 (guàishòu)).

parole.significato: A Japanese business practice of continuous improvement in performance and productivity.
parole.testo: From Japanese 改善 (kaizen かいぜん), from Middle Chinese 改善 (kój-dʒjén) (compare Mandarin gǎishàn 改善), from Old Chinese 改善 (*qˁəʔ-ɡenʔ "to correct errors"), from 改 ("to change") + 善 ("good"). Introduced to English in 1959 by Boyé Lafayette De Mente in his book Japanese Etiquette and Ethics in Business.

parole.significato: A Sino-Japanese word, a Japanese word of Chinese origin or a Japanese word coined along Chinese lines.
parole.testo: From Japanese 漢(かん)語(ご) (kango), from Middle Chinese 漢語 (MC xanH ngjoX, “Han, Chinese + speech, language”), compare modern Mandarin 漢語／汉语 (Hànyǔ, “Chinese language”).

parole.significato: The system of writing Japanese using Chinese characters.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Japanese 漢字(かんじ) (kanji, “Chinese characters”), from Middle Chinese 漢 (MC xanH, “Han dynasty, China”) + Middle Chinese 字 (MC dziH, “[written] character”) (Compare Korean 한자 (hanja), Mandarin 漢字 /汉字 (hànzì), Vietnamese Hán tự, Hokkien 漢字 /汉字 (hàn-jī / hàn-lī), Cantonese 漢字 /汉字 (hon³ zi⁶

parole.significato: The system of writing Japanese kanji using Braille.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Japanese 漢点字(かんてんじ) (kantenji, “Braille kanji”), from Middle Chinese 漢 (MC xanH, “Han dynasty, China”) + Middle Chinese 點 (MC temX, “dot, point”) + Middle Chinese 字 (MC dziH, “[written] character”)

parole.significato: A set of Japanese companies with interlocking business relationships and shareholdings.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Japanese 系列(けいれつ) (keiretsu, literally “system, series”), from Middle Chinese 繫 (ɣèj, “attached”) + 列 (ljet, “set, row”) (compare Mandarin 系列 (xìliè, “series, set”)).

parole.significato: A Japanese martial art using "swords" of split bamboo.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Japanese 剣道 (kendō, “the way of the sword”), from Middle Chinese 劍 (kjæ̀m, “sword”) + 道 (dáu, “way”). Doublet of kumdo.

parole.significato: A robe worn by Buddhist monks and nuns.
parole.testo: From Japanese 袈裟 (けさ, kesa), from Middle Chinese 袈裟 (kˠa ʃˠa), from Sanskrit काषाय (kāṣāya).

parole.significato: Synonym of qilin; typically used in Japanese contexts.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Japanese 麒(き)麟(りん) (kirin), from Middle Chinese. Doublet of qilin.

parole.significato: Any of the kanji characters invented in Japan.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Japanese 国字(こくじ) (kokuji), from Middle Chinese 國 (kwok, “kingdom, nation”) + 字 (dzì, “[written] character”). Doublet of gukja.

parole.significato: A high-ranking member of the yakuza, accountable to the shatei gashira.
parole.testo: From the Japanese 兄弟 (kyōdai きょうだい), from Middle Chinese 兄弟 (xüæng-dèj "brothers"), from Old Chinese 兄弟 (*m̥rang-lˁəjʔ), from 兄 ("elder brother") + 弟 ("younger brother").

parole.significato: A form of traditional Japanese theatre, once performed alongside noh as a comic intermission.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Japanese 狂言 (kyōgen), from Middle Chinese 狂言 (MC gjwang ngjon, “crazed ramblings”)), from 狂 (MC gjwang, “crazy, mad”) + 言 (MC ngjon, “speech”).

parole.significato: A Japanese form of archery.
parole.testo: Japanese 弓道 (kyūdō きゅうどう), from Middle Chinese 弓 (kjuwng "bow") + 道 (dáu "Way").

parole.significato: The highest division of sumo wrestling, above juryo, comprising the yokozuna, ozeki, sekiwake, komusubi and maegashira…
parole.testo: Japanese 幕内 (maku-uchi まくうち, "inside the curtain"), from Middle Chinese 幕 (mak "curtain", "covering") + Japanese うち (uchi "inside").

parole.significato: A form of classical Japanese music drama.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Japanese 能 (nō), from Middle Chinese 能 (nong, “talent, ability”).

parole.significato: Japanese tea, usually green tea.
parole.testo: From Japanese お茶 (ocha), from 御 (o-, honorific prefix) + 茶 (cha, “tea”), from Middle Chinese 茶 (MC drae), whence English cha.

parole.significato: A (Japanese) hot spring.
parole.testo: From Japanese 温泉 (onsen), from Middle Chinese 溫泉 ('won dzjwen, “hot springs”), from 溫 /温 (wēn, “warm”) + 泉 (quán, “spring[s]”). Compare the modern Mandarin pronunciation 溫泉 /温泉 (wēnquán).

parole.significato: A sumo wrestler.
parole.testo: From Japanese 力士(りきし) (rikishi), from Middle Chinese 力士 (lik-dʐí), from Old Chinese 力士 (*k.rək m-s-rəʔ, “man of great strength”), from 力 (*rɯɡ, “strength”) + 士 (*zrɯʔ, “man; soldier”).

parole.significato: A masterless samurai (who often becomes a mercenary to make ends meet).
parole.testo: From Japanese 浪人 (rōnin), in turn from Middle Chinese 浪人 (MC langH nyin, “dissolute, wasteful, unrestrained + person”).

parole.significato: A sudden inexpressible feeling of spiritual awakening or enlightenment, the result of meditation and study.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Japanese 悟り (satori, “understanding; (Buddhism) enlightenment, satori”), from 悟る (satoru, “to perceive; to comprehend, understand; to come to enlightenment”), from Middle Chinese 悟 (nguH, “to become aware, apprehend, realize; to awaken”) (modern Mandarin 悟 (wù)), used to translate Pali

parole.significato: A yokai (“supernatural monster”) having the form of a mind-reading monkey-like creature said to dwell in the mountains…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Japanese 覚 (satori), from Middle Chinese 覺 (kaewk, “to become aware, awaken to, dawn on”) (modern Mandarin 覺 /觉 (jué); referring to the creature’s mind-reading ability).

parole.significato: A Japanese school uniform modelled on the sailor suit.
parole.testo: From Japanese 制服 (seifuku), from Middle Chinese 制服 (MC tsyejH bjuwk).

parole.significato: A voice actor in a native-language version anime, a video game, a radio broadcast or an advertisement in Japan.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Japanese 声優 (seiyū), from Middle Chinese 聲 (*ɕiɛ̝ŋ, “sound, voice”) + 優 (*ʔɨu, “actor”).

parole.significato: A martial arts instructor; especially one for a Japanese martial art.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Japanese 先生(せんせい) (sensei, “teacher; elder”), from Middle Chinese 先生 (MC sen sraeng, “master, elder”), from 先 (MC sen, “earlier, first”) + 生 (MC sraeng, “born”). Compare modern Mandarin 先生 (xiānshēng, “Mr.”). Doublet of sinseh, from Hokkien 先生 (sin-seⁿ).

parole.significato: A form of ritual suicide by disembowelment using a blade, practiced by Japanese samurai, especially to rid oneself of s…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Japanese 切腹 (seppuku), from Middle Chinese 切 (t͡set, “to cut”) + 腹 (pjuwk, “belly”). Compare Cantonese 切腹 (cit³ fuk¹) and Mandarin 切腹 (qiēfù).

parole.significato: A form of massage, using the thumbs and palms, employed as therapy.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Japanese 指(し)圧(あつ) (shiatsu), from Middle Chinese 指 (MC tsyijX, “finger”) + 壓 (MC 'aep, “downward force”).

parole.significato: A dog of a particular breed of Japanese origin.
parole.testo: From Japanese 四国 (しこく, Shikoku, “four provinces”), from Middle Chinese 四 (sìj, “four”) + 國 (kwok, “state”, “country”). (dog): < Japanese 四国犬 (shikoku-inu, “Shikoku dog”), named after the island where they originated.

parole.significato: the four judges, sitting at each cardinal point
parole.testo: From Japanese 審判 (shinpan, しんぱん), from Middle Chinese 審判 (ʃim-pʰàn "to judge", "to try") (compare Mandarin shěnpàn 审判).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to, Shintoism.
parole.testo: Borrowing from Japanese 神道 (Shintō), from Middle Chinese 神道 (MC zyin dawX, “ways of the gods”), ultimately from Old Chinese 神道 (OC *hlin l'uːʔ, “ways [doings] of Heaven [in matters of fortune or fate]”).

parole.significato: A Japanese alcoholic beverage, most commonly distilled from barley, sweet potato or rice. Typically it is 25% alcohol b…
parole.testo: From Japanese 焼(しょう)酎(ちゅう) (shōchū), from Middle Chinese 燒酒 (syew tsjuw^X), from 燒 /烧 (shāo, “burn; flammable”) + 酒 (jiǔ, “alcohol”). Compare Mandarin 烧酒 (shāojiǔ), and Korean 소주 (soju). Doublet of shaojiu and soju.

parole.significato: A style of Japanese erotic art
parole.testo: From Japanese 春画, from Middle Chinese 春 (t͡ʃʰwin "spring", by extension "sexual", "erotic") + 畫 (hwɛ̀ "painting").

parole.significato: A dart or throwing blade, sometimes with multiple points, used as a weapon by ninja (or samurai).
parole.testo: From Japanese 手裏剣 (しゅりけん shuriken), from Middle Chinese 手 (ʃúw "hand") + 裏 (lí "inside") + 劍 (kjæ̀m "sword").

parole.significato: The calm, straight-backed squat, following the shiko exercises, in mental preparation for the tachiai
parole.testo: From Japanese 蹲踞 (sonkyo), from Middle Chinese 蹲踞 (MC dzwon kjoH).

parole.significato: A form of Japanese verse in five lines of 5, 7, 5, 7, and 7 morae.
parole.testo: From Japanese 短歌 (tanka, “short song”), from Middle Chinese 短 (MC twanX) 歌 (MC ka) (compare Mandarin 短歌 (duǎngē) duǎngē).

parole.significato: A traditional Japanese small sword or knife; often used as a secondary weapon to a katana.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Japanese 短刀 (tantō), from Middle Chinese 短刀 (twan^X taw, “dagger”).

parole.significato: The emperor of Japan as head of state and the head of the Japanese imperial family.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Japanese 天皇(てんのう) (tennō), from Middle Chinese 天皇 (then hwang) with the original sense of “heavenly sovereign”.

parole.significato: A protein-rich food made from curdled soy milk.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Japanese 豆(とう)腐(ふ) (tōfu), from Middle Chinese 豆腐 (duwᴴ bju^X, “curdled bean”). Doublet of dubu and doufu.

parole.significato: A Japanese wheat noodle.
parole.testo: From Japanese 饂飩 (udon), which is probably from Middle Chinese 餛飩 (hwon dwon, “wonton”).

parole.significato: A range of appearances, mannerisms, or behaviors of a humanoid figure that are subtly different from a human and thereb…
parole.testo: Calque of Japanese 不気味の谷 (bukimi no tani), from 不気味 (bukimi, “eerie, uncanny”, of Middle Chinese origin, literally “bad taste and smell”) + の (no, noun modifier particle) + 谷 (tani, “valley”). First used in 1970 by roboticist Masahiro Mori.

parole.significato: Any of several Japanese breeds of cattle genetically predisposed to intense marbling and to producing a high percentage…
parole.testo: From Japanese 和(わ)牛(ぎゅう) (wagyū), from Middle Chinese 和 (MC hwa, “a gloss for 倭 (MC 'wa, “Japan”)”) + 牛 (MC ngjuw, “cow”).

parole.significato: A kind of classical Japanese poem.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Japanese 和歌 (waka), from Middle Chinese 和 (ɣwa), a gloss for 倭 (ʔwa, “Japan”) + 歌 (ka, “song”).

parole.significato: A Japanese room with tatami flooring and usually sliding doors.
parole.testo: From Japanese 和室 (washitsu わしつ), from Middle Chinese 和 (ɣwa, a gloss for ʔwa 倭 "Japan") + 室 (ʃit "room").

parole.significato: Any of various supernatural monsters, sometimes shapeshifters, in Japanese folklore.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Japanese 妖怪 (yōkai, “ghost, phantom, monster”), from Middle Chinese 妖怪 ('jew kweajᴴ) with the similar meaning.

parole.significato: A style of Western-influenced Japanese cuisine.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Japanese 洋食 (yōshoku), from Middle Chinese 洋 (yáng "ocean", by extension "foreign", "Western") + 食 (ʒik "eat", "food").

parole.significato: A large business conglomerate founded under the Empire of Japan, generally controlled by a single family or individual.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Japanese 財閥(ざいばつ) (zaibatsu), coined from Middle Chinese 財 (d͡zoj, “wealth”) + 閥 (bjot, “powerful family”).
